lead: A complex pole at −σ ± jω gives a term e^(−σt)cos(ωt + φ), where σ is how far the pole sits left of the jω axis. A real pole at −σ gives only e^(−σt). A pole close to the axis decays slowly and keeps influencing the response; a pole far left dies quickly. Relative stability measures that distance. The pole or pair nearest the axis, the dominant poles, fixes the settling time and overshoot: a complex pair if the nearest poles are complex, a single real pole if a real pole sits closest. Engineers use this to judge a design, choose a gain, and decide whether a small change in a pole or zero will slow or speed up a drive, a power supply, or a control loop.
prereq: You need 3.2 for the Routh test on a shifted polynomial, and Unit 2 for second-order step response, ζ, ωn, settling time and peak overshoot.

sections.h3: Relative stability is distance from the jω axis

blocks.text: BIBO stability only says every closed-loop pole is left of the jω axis. It does not say how far left. A pole p = −σ + jω gives a term e^(−σt)cos(ωt), where σ > 0 is the distance from the axis in rad/s and the real part is −σ. Small σ means slow decay. Relative stability measures this margin.
To test whether every pole is left of the line s = −σ, shift the origin. Put s = z − σ, so z = s + σ. The line s = −σ becomes z = 0. Expand D(s) in z:

blocks.where: D(s) is the characteristic polynomial; D_σ(z) is the same polynomial after the shift; a_n … a_0 are its new real coefficients.

blocks.text: All s-poles lie strictly left of s = −σ exactly when every root of D_σ(z) has negative real part. Run the Routh array of 3.2 on D_σ(z). No sign change in the first column means margin at least σ; each sign change counts roots to the right of the line. Increase σ until the array turns marginal. That largest σ is the distance of the nearest pole.

sections.h3: Dominant poles and the second-order estimate

blocks.text: Not all poles shape the response equally. The term e^(−σt) dies; the pole with smallest σ lasts longest. A complex pair nearest the axis is the dominant pair when every other pole is at least five times farther left and its residue, the weight in the partial-fraction expansion, is small. The five-times rule is a rule of thumb, not a theorem.

For a dominant pair at −ζωn ± jωn√(1 − ζ²), ζ is the damping ratio and ωn is the natural frequency in rad/s. The damped frequency is ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²). The second-order approximation is T(s) ≈ Kωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²), where K is the DC gain of the closed-loop system, so T(0) = K; the denominator carries ζ and ωn.

blocks.where: t_s is the 2% settling time in seconds; M_p is peak overshoot as a fraction; ζ is dimensionless; valid for 0 < ζ < 1.

blocks.text: Use these numbers only after the dominance check. A pole at −3 next to a pair at −1 ± j3 is only three times farther and changes both settling and overshoot. The pair-only formulas can then be too optimistic about speed.

sections.h3: Effect of an added pole or zero

blocks.text: Adding an open-loop real pole, such as a sensor lag, adds a branch to the root locus. In a typical low-order loop the locus bends right, the dominant pair moves closer to the jω axis or to a lower damping ratio, the response slows, and overshoot usually rises. The extra closed-loop real pole can partly mask this, but the trend is lower relative stability, not higher. Adding an open-loop zero bends the locus left, acts like derivative action, speeds the response, and usually raises overshoot. These are trends, not guarantees; confirm on the 3.4 locus.

If a zero is close to a pole, their partial-fraction contributions largely cancel. The mode is weak but not gone unless the positions are exactly equal. In a transfer function this looks harmless; in hardware an unstable hidden pole can still drift, so do not rely on cancelling a right-half-plane pole.

figure.caption: The envelopes show how a pole at −σ decays; the σ = 1 curve crosses the 2% band at 4 s and σ = 2 at 2 s, so doubling the distance from the axis halves settling.

spec.aria: Two decaying envelopes with a horizontal 2% line; the envelope for σ = 1 crosses the band at t = 4 s while the one for σ = 2 crosses it at t = 2 s.

examples.question: A unity-feedback system has closed-loop transfer function T(s) = 100/((s + 10)(s² + 2s + 10)). (a) Find all poles. (b) Name the dominant pair and give ζ and ωn. (c) Estimate the 2% settling time and the peak overshoot.
steps: One pole is s = −10. For the quadratic s² + 2s + 10 = 0, s = [−2 ± √(4 − 40)]/2 = −1 ± j3.
The pair −1 ± j3 is nearest the jω axis. The real pole at −10 is 10/1 = 10 times farther left, more than five times, so the pair is dominant.
Compare −1 ± j3 with −ζωn ± jωn√(1 − ζ²). Then ζωn = 1 and ωn√(1 − ζ²) = 3, so ωn² = 1² + 3² = 10 and ωn = 3.162 rad/s. ζ = 1/ωn = 1/√10 = 0.316.
examples.answer: The poles are −10 and −1 ± j3; the dominant pair gives ωn = 3.162 rad/s and ζ = 0.316, with 2% settling time ≈ 4.0 s and peak overshoot ≈ 0.3509 (35.1%).
examples.check:
import math
wn = math.sqrt(10)
zeta = 1/math.sqrt(10)
ts = 4/(zeta*wn)
mp = math.exp(-math.pi*zeta/math.sqrt(1-zeta*zeta))
print(round(wn, 4))
print(round(zeta, 4))
print(round(ts, 4))
print(round(mp, 4))

traps: Calling a complex pair dominant just because it is the only pair, when a real pole sits two or three times closer to the jω axis.
Quoting overshoot from ζ before checking that every neglected pole is at least about five times farther left and has a small residue.
Treating a stable pole at −0.2 as good enough: it is stable, but its slow decay gives a long settling time and weak relative stability.
Reversing the shift: s = z − σ moves the line s = −σ to z = 0, and all roots must lie left of z = 0, not right.
Assuming every added zero improves the response; a zero can speed the loop but also raise overshoot and reduce damping.

quiz.q: Define relative stability and state which pole property fixes it.
quiz.a: Relative stability is how far the closed-loop poles lie left of the jω axis. The real part of the pole nearest the axis fixes the slowest decay and therefore the margin.

quiz.q: A stable system has poles at −0.1 ± j8. Why can its response still be sluggish?
quiz.a: Stability needs only a negative real part. The decay rate is σ = 0.1 rad/s, so the 2% settling time is roughly 4/0.1 = 40 s. The large imaginary part gives fast oscillation, not fast settling.

quiz.q: A system has poles at −2 ± j4 and a real pole at −12. Estimate ζ, ωn, the 2% settling time, and the peak overshoot from the dominant pair.
quiz.a: For the pair, ζωn = 2 and ωn√(1 − ζ²) = 4, so ωn² = 20, ωn = 4.472 rad/s, ζ = 2/4.472 = 0.447. Settling time ≈ 4/2 = 2 s. Overshoot ≈ e^(−π × 0.447/√(1 − 0.2)) = e^(−1.571) = 0.208, about 20.8%. The real pole at −12 is six times farther left, so the estimate is reasonable.

quiz.q: For D(s) = s² + 4s + 8, use the shift s = z − 1 and Routh's test to decide whether all roots lie left of s = −1.
quiz.a: Substitute s = z − 1: D(z − 1) = (z − 1)² + 4(z − 1) + 8 = z² + 2z + 5. The Routh first column is 1, 2, 5, all positive, so all z-roots are left of z = 0. Therefore all s-roots are left of s = −1.

quiz.q: A system has a dominant pair at −1 ± j3 and a real pole at −3. A student uses the second-order formulas. Is the estimate reliable? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The real pole is only three times farther left, less than the five-times rule of thumb, and its residue may not be small. The pair-only settling and overshoot values can be wrong; use the full third-order response.

quiz.q: Why can a zero placed very close to a slow pole make a root-locus design look better than the hardware behaves?
quiz.a: The zero and pole almost cancel, so the slow mode has a small residue in the transfer function and is barely visible. Unless the positions are exactly equal, the mode still exists. In hardware, an unstable or poorly damped hidden state can drift even when the input-output response looks clean.

beyond: Not for the exam. Model-order reduction uses the same idea: keep the slow dominant modes and discard fast ones, with balanced truncation giving an error bound. In digital control, sampling adds poles that can become dominant even when the continuous design looks fast. In power electronics, a slow thermal or battery pole often sets the outer-loop bandwidth, so designers check it before tuning the current loop. Search next for dominant pole approximation, model order reduction, balanced truncation, and pole-zero cancellation in robust control.
